1.title: Security Awareness and Measuring Cybersecurity Effectiveness
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Security Awareness and Measuring Cybersecurity Effectiveness. It covers the exam area two. Security Governance. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. two point three Understand security awareness: Organizational culture (for example importance of security, security leadership). Concepts (for example social engineering, password protection, phishing). two point four Measure cybersecurity effectiveness: Key metrics, Key Risk Indicators (K R I). Dashboards, score cards, reports. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: two. Security Governance (seventeen point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Awareness, training and education
1.text: Awareness, training and education. People are both the weakest link and the best sensor. A good program builds habits. Awareness. Audience and aim: Everyone; recognize a risk and report it. Example: A short yearly course, posters, phishing tips. Training. Audience and aim: A role; build skills to do a task securely. Example: Secure coding for developers. Education. Audience and aim: Career depth; deep knowledge. Example: A degree or advanced course.

1.title: Organizational culture and leadership
1.text: Organizational culture and leadership. A security culture means that security is part of how people work. Tone from the top. Leaders follow the rules themselves and fund security. Security leadership. A named leader, such as a chief information security officer (see so), sets direction. No-blame reporting. People report mistakes and suspicious messages without fear. Security champions. Volunteers in each team who spread good practice. Exam tip: Culture starts with leaders. If staff fear punishment for reporting a click on a phishing link, incidents stay hidden.

1.title: Social engineering and phishing
1.text: Social engineering and phishing. Social engineering tricks people into giving access or information. It attacks the human, not the software.

1.title: Social engineering and phishing, continued
1.text: Social engineering and phishing. The figure shows this: Common social engineering attacks and the channel each uses.

1.title: Social engineering and phishing, continued
1.text: Social engineering and phishing. Phishing. Fake email that asks for data or a click, sent to many people. Spear phishing. Targeted at one person or group, using personal details. Whaling. Spear phishing aimed at executives. Vishing. Voice call (phone). Smishing. Text message (S M S). Pretexting. An invented story to gain trust and information. Baiting. A tempting item, such as an infected U S B drive left lying around. Tailgating (piggybacking). Following an authorized person through a secured door. Shoulder surfing, dumpster diving. Watching a screen; searching trash for secrets.

1.title: Social engineering and phishing, continued
1.text: Social engineering and phishing. Red flags: urgency, unexpected request, mismatched sender or link, pressure to bypass the process, requests for credentials or payment. Report it; do not click. A I raises the stakes: attackers use A I to write convincing phishing, clone voices and make deepfake video calls, so verify through a second channel.

1.title: Password protection
1.text: Password protection. Long, unique passwords (a passphrase). Length beats complexity; reuse spreads a breach. Password manager. Lets you use a different strong password everywhere. Multi-factor authentication. A stolen password alone is not enough. Never share or write passwords in plain sight. Accounts must be traceable to one person. Exam tip: Phishing is many, spear phishing is one, whaling is the executive. Tailgating is physical; phishing is email.

1.title: Measuring effectiveness
1.text: Measuring effectiveness. You cannot manage what you do not measure. Metrics show whether controls work. Metric. Meaning: A measurement. Example: Number of phishing emails reported. Key performance indicator (K P I). Meaning: Shows how well you meet a goal. Example: Patch compliance of ninety-five percent against a target of ninety-eight. Key risk indicator (K R I). Meaning: An early warning that risk is rising. Example: Growing count of overdue critical patches; spike in failed logins.

1.title: Measuring effectiveness, continued
1.text: Measuring effectiveness. Typical security metrics: phishing simulation click rate and report rate, mean time to detect (M T T D), mean time to respond (M T T R), number of incidents, open vulnerabilities by age, training completion. A I-specific K R Is include model drift and A I-assisted attack attempts. Dashboard. Live or frequent view of key numbers, for operations. Scorecard. Compares results with targets over time, for managers. Report. Detailed, periodic write-up for leaders and auditors. Exam tip: K P I looks back at performance; K R I looks ahead at danger. Pick the dashboard for live view, the report for detail.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An email addressed to the chief financial officer by name refers to a real project and asks for an urgent wire transfer. What attack is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Whaling, a targeted phishing attack on an executive. A targeted phishing attack aimed at a senior executive is whaling.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A caller claims to be from the help desk and asks an employee to read out a six-digit code. Which attack is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Vishing, because it uses a voice call. A phone call that tries to trick the victim is vishing.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An unknown person walks into a secured office behind an employee who holds the door. What is this called? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Tailgating, following into a secured area. Following an authorized person through a secured door is tailgating.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which measure is a key risk indicator rather than a performance indicator? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A rising number of overdue critical patches. A K R I is an early warning that risk is rising, such as growing overdue critical patches.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A security manager wants a quick, live view of alerts and open incidents for the operations team. Which format fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A dashboard with current key numbers. A dashboard gives a live or frequent view of key numbers for operations.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Staff receive a video call that looks like the chief executive and asks for a payment. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Verify the request through a second, known channel. A I can fake voices and video, so verify through a separate known channel and report it.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is phishing sent to one person called? Answer: Spear phishing. Question two. What does S M S-based phishing have as a name? Answer: Smishing. Question three. What is the difference between a K P I and a K R I? Answer: A K P I shows performance against a goal; a K R I warns that risk is rising.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Who is the audience of awareness training? Answer: Everyone in the organization. Question five. What does tone from the top mean? Answer: Leaders follow and fund the security rules themselves. Question six. What does a password manager enable? Answer: A different strong password for every account.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Levels: awareness (all), training (role), education (depth). Culture: tone from the top, see so, no-blame reporting, champions. Attacks: phishing, spear, whaling, vishing, smishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating. A I: convincing phishing, voice cloning, deepfakes; verify by a second channel. Measures: K P I (performance), K R I (early warning), M T T D, M T T R. Formats: dashboard (live), scorecard (targets), report (detail).
